docs.title: compose-api
docs.text: An API server for reproducible biological workflows and cosimulations.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Optional. Omitting Authorization leaves the request anonymous. A bad bearer token is 401, not an anonymous call. GET /health and GET /version ignore the header. A valid access token identifies the caller and does not make a simulation private.

How to obtain an access token, which audience to use, and what not to send: Authentication.

docs.title: Command-line client
docs.text: compose-api signs you in through Auth0 and calls this API from a terminal: the simulator catalog, a simulation's status, and new submissions. Installation, profiles, sessions and exit codes: Command-line client.

docs.title: Calling the Compose API
docs.text: Authentication is optional on the existing business endpoints. The API accepts anonymous requests there, and a valid access token identifies who is calling. It does not change which simulations, statuses, or result files you can read. GET /auth/me requires authentication.

docs.title: Verify the authenticated identity
docs.text:
GET /auth/me requires a valid Compose-audience bearer access token. It returns issuer, subject, audience, roles, scopes, and permissions, with sorted arrays and Cache-Control: no-store. It never returns the token, email, or other account/profile details. Use (issuer, subject) as the identity key, not email.

Missing or invalid credentials receive the same 401 and WWW-Authenticate: Bearer described below. A valid machine token also works: this endpoint reflects the existing principal contract, not a human-only restriction. The generated client's get_current_principal operation requires AuthenticatedClient; existing business operations still accept either Client or AuthenticatedClient.

This endpoint proves server recognition of a credential; it does not prove persisted Auth0 role membership or grant ownership of simulations. The compose-api CLI uses it to confirm a sign-in (see "CLI sessions" below). Native-client infrastructure and live provider validation have separate deployment gates.

docs.title: Authentication at a glance
docs.text:
Omit the Authorization header and the request is anonymous.

Send one header when you want the call attributed to an authenticated caller:

Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>

<ACCESS_TOKEN> must be an OAuth access token for this API (see below). The scheme is case-insensitive (Bearer and bearer both work). Send the header once.

A header that is present but not acceptable is 401 Unauthorized. The body is {"detail": "Invalid authentication credentials"}, with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer. The API does not fall back to anonymous. That includes:

  • a scheme other than Bearer, an empty token, or more than one Authorization header
  • a malformed token, a bad signature, or an algorithm other than RS256
  • an expired token, or a token whose issuer or audience does not match this server

To call anonymously, leave the header out.

GET /health and GET /version ignore the header. A missing, valid, or garbage Authorization value still returns 200.

docs.title: Authentication does not make a simulation private
docs.text:
A valid access token identifies the caller. It does not attach the simulation to that caller, and it does not hide the simulation from anyone else.

Every route that reads something a simulation owns asks the server's read policy whether the caller may read it, and the verified caller is the one it asks about:

  • GET /results/simulation/status?simulation_id=<id>
  • GET /results/simulations/status/batch
  • GET /results/simulation/results/file?simulation_id=<id>
  • GET /results/simulation/events, GET /results/simulation/trace and GET /results/simulation/trace/chrome
  • GET /simulations and GET /simulations/<id>
  • GET /datasets, GET /datasets/<id>, GET /datasets/<id>/content and GET /datasets/<id>/files/<subpath>
  • GET /comparisons, GET /comparisons/<id> and GET /comparisons/<id>/series, readable only when every run in the comparison is readable by the caller

The policy lets anyone read a public simulation, and only its owner read a private one. A deployment can also let one role read every private simulation by setting ADMIN_ROLE (Settings.admin_role); it is empty by default, so no role does. It refuses user, the role every signed-in caller holds, so a deployment configured with it fails to start. Submitting a simulation does not record an owner yet, so every simulation is public. Anyone who has the id can read its status, events and datasets and, when the results file exists, download it. Anonymous and authenticated callers see the same record. A missing simulation, or results that are not ready yet, is 404.

Do not treat bearer authentication as an access-control boundary for simulation status or results.

docs.title: Human callers
docs.text:
This API does not register or sign in users; Auth0 does. There are three supported ways for a person to get an access token for it:

  • The compose-api command-line client. It signs you up or in on Auth0's hosted pages (email and password, or Google), keeps the session in your operating system's credential store, renews it, and calls this API for you.
  • The web UI at /ui. "Sign in" runs Auth0's Authorization Code flow with PKCE in the browser, with this API's audience; the UI sends the token only to this API, and asks GET /auth/me who you are and what you may do.
  • BioSim's web login. The client that completed that login requests an access token whose audience is the Compose API identifier for the environment you are calling, and sends it in the Authorization header above.

When that client holds a refresh token, use the client's refresh flow to obtain a new access token before the current one expires. Send the new access token to this API. Do not send the refresh token here. This API does not issue, refresh, or revoke tokens.

docs.title: Service callers
docs.text:
A service uses the OAuth 2.0 client-credentials grant. The Auth0 application must be allowed to request the Compose API audience for that environment. Ask the tenant for a new access token when the current one expires. Client credentials do not return a refresh token.

curl --request POST \
  --url "https://<AUTH0_DOMAIN>/oauth/token" \
  --header "content-type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "grant_type": "client_credentials",
    "client_id": "<CLIENT_ID>",
    "client_secret": "<CLIENT_SECRET>",
    "audience": "<COMPOSE_API_AUDIENCE>"
  }'

Use the access_token from the response as <ACCESS_TOKEN>. <AUTH0_DOMAIN> is the bare host configured on the server (AUTH0_DOMAIN, no https:// and no trailing slash). <COMPOSE_API_AUDIENCE> is that server's AUTH0_AUDIENCE.

docs.title: Local and production audiences
docs.text:
The audience is the API identifier the token was issued for. It is not the URL you call.

The checked-in deployments expect:

Environment API host AUTH0_AUDIENCE Production (kustomize/config/compose-api-rke/api.env) https://compose.cam.uchc.edu https://api.compose.cam.uchc.edu Local cluster (kustomize/overlays/compose-api-local/ingress.yaml, auth0.env) https://api.compose-api-local https://api.compose.local

Those two audiences are not interchangeable. A token minted for one is rejected by a server configured with the other. Both of those deployments currently use the same AUTH0_DOMAIN (dev-bu7yo7484tyxu6a1.us.auth0.com); sharing a tenant does not make the audiences interchangeable.

A server started from assets/dev/config/.dev_env uses whatever AUTH0_AUDIENCE is set there. Match the token to that value.

docs.title: When Auth0 is not configured
docs.text:
AUTH0_DOMAIN and AUTH0_AUDIENCE are ordinary settings, not secrets. If either one is empty, or both are, verification is off. The two cases behave the same:

  • a request with no Authorization header still succeeds as anonymous
  • a request that sends a bearer token receives the same 401 as any other rejected credential

/health and /version are unchanged.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
A verified caller is recorded with the role user. If the access token includes the https://api.biosimulations.org/roles claim (tokens for a person signed in through BioSim, the CLI or the web UI do; client-credentials tokens do not), those role names are recorded as well. An anonymous caller has no role.

Roles identify the caller. Three settings name the roles this API checks; each is empty by default, which turns its check off, and none may be user, the role every signed-in caller holds:

Setting Grants Production ENVIRONMENT_ADMIN_ROLE create, default, retire and read back environment versions admin SUITE_CURATOR_ROLE mark, edit and clear a suite's known problems admin ADMIN_ROLE read every private simulation unset

The shared BioSim admin role grants only what a deployment names it for. No simulation is private yet, so today no role changes what a caller can read. Do not assume any other role grants or denies access unless this API documents that check.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
GET /auth/me returns, beside the roles, capabilities: what this deployment lets the caller do, by name. Each is computed by the same function that enforces it (compose_api/authorization.py, CAPABILITIES), so the two cannot disagree, and a client shows controls by capability rather than by matching role names, which are server configuration.

Capability Held by a caller with environments:admin ENVIRONMENT_ADMIN_ROLE suites:curate SUITE_CURATOR_ROLE simulations:read-all ADMIN_ROLE

compose-api auth status --verify prints them. The list is empty for a caller with none of the roles; an anonymous caller has no /auth/me. A capability only says what the API will accept: every request is checked again.

docs.title: Do not
docs.text:
Do not use the Resource Owner Password Credentials grant (the password grant). Collecting a user's password in your client is not a supported way to call this API. Human callers sign in through the compose-api CLI or BioSim, on Auth0's own pages, and send the resulting access token. Services use client credentials.

Do not send an ID token. An ID token's audience is the client application, not the Compose API, so this API rejects it. Send the access token whose audience is the Compose API identifier for the environment you are calling.

docs.title: CLI sessions and local logout
docs.text:
The native CLI's auth login and auth signup persist a validated session in an approved OS credential store. Public profiles are separate from server configuration. Configure the native client ID in the CLI profile before signing in. The CLI never accepts passwords or tokens as command arguments and never falls back to a token file.

compose-api auth status inspects local expiry without contacting Auth0 or renewing credentials; --json emits non-secret metadata. A local identity is not proof of current API access, so the output labels the API's last confirmation as a stored fact. auth status --verify renews the session if needed and asks GET /auth/me; a network failure there is reported as such, not as a sign-out. Sign-in ends with the same check: it succeeds only once the API has confirmed the identity, and if the API cannot be reached it keeps the saved session, says it is unconfirmed and exits non-zero.

Every API command (compose-api run, status, simulations list, ...) sends the profile's stored session when there is one, and calls anonymously when there is none, as the API allows; none starts a sign-in on its own. A credential store that exists but cannot be read (locked, corrupt) is an error, never an anonymous call: a signed-in person's submission is never silently sent unowned. A read the API rejects with 401 is renewed and retried once; a 403 is final. A submission is never sent twice: after a timeout or server error its outcome is reported as unknown. The bearer is sent only to the profile's API origin, never to Auth0 or a redirect, and not at all when --url names another API. Error messages name the operation and the HTTP status, not text from the server.

compose-api auth logout attempts bounded refresh-token revocation, then deletes local credentials even when the provider is unavailable. --local-only performs only local deletion. Revocation failure is reported with exit 5; failed local deletion is exit 6 and must be retried after unlocking/repairing the OS store. No secret is retained in a revocation retry queue. Already-issued access tokens can remain valid until expiry, and neither command clears Auth0 or Google browser sessions.

Access and refresh tokens live together in one versioned keyring record. The service identifier begins with compose-api.cli.v1. and ends in the public configuration binding digest; it contains no email. A changed issuer, client, audience, API origin or requested scope set selects a different session. Identical profile bindings share a session deliberately. macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service and Windows Credential Manager are allowlisted. On Windows the CLI writes and reads its item natively, with a single overwrite and no keyring shadow copy, and stores the record as UTF-8: an item holds 2560 bytes, and a realistic session is about 1700 as UTF-8 but twice that as the UTF-16 keyring writes (#320). The rest of the item is room for the access token's claims: six roles and sixteen RBAC permissions bring a session to about 2250 bytes, and each further short permission adds about 25. A record that outgrows the item is refused, never split; the refusal comes after the sign-in, so it points to --ephemeral-auth. Unknown, chained, plaintext and null backends are refused. Keyrings protect credentials at rest, not against a compromised operating-system account. Python cannot promise memory zeroization.

Non-secret lock/generation/journal files live under the platform user-state directory, in compose-api/sessions. POSIX directories/files require 0700/0600 and current-user ownership. Windows uses a protected owner-only ACL. Do not delete these files to reset a session while another command is running: retained generation tombstones prevent a late login callback from resurrecting a logged-out session. Use auth logout --local-only instead. Corrupt credential records and corrupt private metadata are removable through local logout; unsafe file ownership, permissions or symlinks must be repaired by the local user first.

Refresh holds the binding's process lock and journals the attempt before any provider request. Other processes reread the successor rather than rotate twice. If Auth0 cannot even be discovered, the refresh token was not sent and the session stays. Once the refresh request may have left the machine, a crash or a failed answer with no durably stored successor requires a fresh sign-in; the old refresh credential is never replayed. An already stored complete successor can recover an interrupted metadata cleanup. Login uses a separate transaction lock and commits only if its starting generation still matches. A failed/locked backend stops persistent sign-in before the browser when detectable; there is no insecure fallback. On a host without a usable credential store, put --ephemeral-auth before an API command (compose-api --ephemeral-auth run x.omex): it signs in for that one command, requests no refresh token, keeps the session in memory and forgets it when the command ends.

Real stores are exercised by tests/cli/test_os_keyring.py (opt-in: COMPOSE_API_TEST_OS_KEYRING=1, synthetic records under random names, always deleted). On 2026-10-07 it passed against the macOS Keychain (macOS 27.0.1) and GNOME Keyring's Secret Service (Debian 13, in a container), where a locked keyring was also refused before sign-in. On 2026-10-16 it passed against Windows Credential Manager (Windows Server 2025, GitHub's windows-latest runner, in the CLI platforms workflow, which runs it on every client change): a realistic session of each length parity was saved, reloaded and found as UTF-8 in one item, and a renewal was read back as the successor. Crash paths use deterministic fakes. Credential Manager and its ACLs on a real Windows desktop, and live refresh and revocation driven by the CLI, remain release gates; a CI runner and passing mocks do not close them.

docs.title: The compose-api command line
docs.text:
compose-api drives the compose-api service from a terminal or a script: sign up or in through Auth0 in your browser, keep the session in your operating system's credential store, submit simulations, wait for them, fetch their results, and inspect what the service has registered. It covers every operation in the API (a test fails if an operation is added without a command). How it is built and why: plan-cli.md.

Signing in identifies you to the API. It does not make your simulations private: anyone with a simulation's numeric ID can read its status and results (see Authentication). Roles are labels on your identity, not access controls on simulations.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
$ pip install 'compose-api-client[cli]'      # or: uv tool install 'compose-api-client[cli]'
$ compose-api --help

The base package (pip install compose-api-client) is the Python client alone: httpx, attrs and python-dateutil, no server dependencies. The [auth] extra adds the Auth0 / keyring session layer, and [cli] includes [auth] plus the terminal UI. In this repository, uv run compose-api ... works with no install.

docs.title: Connect and Profiles
docs.text:
Setting Option Environment Default Profile --profile COMPOSE_API_CLI_PROFILE production Service --url COMPOSE_API_URL the selected profile's api_base_url HTTP timeout --timeout COMPOSE_API_TIMEOUT 300 s (downloads; other requests cap at 60 s) Output -o/--output auto\|table\|json COMPOSE_API_OUTPUT auto: a table on a terminal, JSON when piped Automation token — (env-only) COMPOSE_API_TOKEN none (uses stored session, else anonymous)

Global options go before the command: compose-api -o json status 4192. Results go to stdout; progress lines and errors go to stderr, so compose-api -o json ... | jq always sees clean JSON.

A profile says which API to call and how to sign in to it. Two are built in:

Profile API Auth0 audience Client ID production (default) https://compose.cam.uchc.edu https://api.compose.cam.uchc.edu 1FV43fysEjhTrYYRNaMEGvCteu4g2ay4 local https://api.compose-api-local https://api.compose.local Fp3QmULWNIhdutlBRVFm2HjPGapqdnKV

Both use the tenant dev-bu7yo7484tyxu6a1.us.auth0.com, the database connection Username-Password-Authentication, the Google connection google-oauth2 and callback port 8400. The client IDs belong to public native applications: they are identifiers, not secrets, and there is no client secret anywhere in the CLI.

Choose a profile with --profile NAME or COMPOSE_API_CLI_PROFILE. Each setting is then taken from its environment variable, else from [profiles.<name>] in config.toml (under your user configuration directory), else from the built-in value. compose-api config show prints every effective value and where it came from.

Setting Environment variable Meaning api_base_url COMPOSE_API_CLI_API_BASE_URL The API origin. https only, except a loopback host (http://localhost:8000). No path, query or credentials. auth0_domain COMPOSE_API_CLI_AUTH0_DOMAIN The tenant's bare host. The issuer is derived from it. auth0_audience COMPOSE_API_CLI_AUTH0_AUDIENCE The API identifier, exactly as the server's AUTH0_AUDIENCE. It is not the URL you call. auth0_client_id COMPOSE_API_CLI_AUTH0_CLIENT_ID The native application's public client ID. database_connection COMPOSE_API_CLI_DATABASE_CONNECTION Optional: steers --provider email to this connection. google_connection COMPOSE_API_CLI_GOOGLE_CONNECTION Needed for --provider google in the browser. callback_port COMPOSE_API_CLI_CALLBACK_PORT The registered loopback callback port, http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback. Default 8400. ca_bundle COMPOSE_API_CLI_CA_BUNDLE Absolute path to extra CA certificates (PEM) for an API with a private CA.

docs.title: Sign up and sign in
docs.text:
Passwords, MFA, email verification and Google consent all happen on Auth0's pages in your own browser. The CLI never asks for a password, and never accepts a password or --token flag on the command line.

compose-api auth signup                     # create an email-and-password account
compose-api auth signup --provider google   # first sign-in with Google creates the account
compose-api auth login                      # returning user: choose email or Google on the page
compose-api auth login --provider google
compose-api auth login --method device      # sign in on another device (SSH, containers)
compose-api auth status                     # what is stored locally; contacts nothing
compose-api auth status --verify            # renews if needed and asks GET /auth/me to confirm the identity
compose-api auth logout                     # revokes the refresh token with Auth0, then erases the session
compose-api auth logout --local-only

--method chooses how a sign-in reaches you: auto (the default) picks from the environment: the device code over SSH (SSH_CONNECTION), on a headless host or in a GitHub Codespace, and the browser otherwise. Over SSH or without a display, a recognized VS Code bin/helpers/browser.sh or browser.cmd helper, or WSL's wslview, still gets the browser, since they forward the callback port. VS Code or WSL environment markers alone do not qualify: a text browser, an unknown command or a fallback list in $BROWSER gets the device code. An unrecognized helper can still be chosen explicitly with --method browser. A Codespace still gets the device code, because one opened in a web browser cannot receive the callback. Whenever auto picks anything but your desktop's browser, the command says why and how to choose another way. browser opens the system browser, or $BROWSER without a display. A text browser there (w3m, lynx, links, elinks, www-browser) would take over the terminal, so it counts as none and the command says to use url or device. url prints the sign-in link instead of opening anything; device is RFC 8628, for signing in on another device. The same option works with --ephemeral-auth before any command.

The session is one record in your operating system's credential store (macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service or Windows Credential Manager), under compose-api.cli.v1.<digest>. Plaintext and unknown keyring backends are refused; there is no file fallback. On hosts without a credential store, use --ephemeral-auth before the command (for example compose-api --ephemeral-auth --method device simulators list), which signs in for a single command in memory without requesting a refresh token.

The browser flow listens on http://127.0.0.1:8400/callback, the only callback the tenant's applications register, so COMPOSE_API_CLI_CALLBACK_PORT cannot move it. If port 8400 is already in use, sign-in stops before the browser opens; over SSH, ssh -L 8400:127.0.0.1:8400 forwards the callback to your own computer, which makes --method url work there.

For CI and non-interactive automation, set COMPOSE_API_TOKEN in the environment. When set, it takes precedence over a stored session for the active profile (printing a one-line notice to stderr), is never renewed or printed, and is still bound by the destination guard (_DestinationGuard), redirect refusal (follow_redirects=False) and environment isolation (trust_env=False). If --url is overridden to an origin different from the profile's api_base_url, neither a stored session nor COMPOSE_API_TOKEN is sent to it.

docs.title: A run, start to finish
docs.text:
$ compose-api run experiment.omex --simulator viva-pde-particle --wait --download out/ --extract
submitted simulation 4195
    0s simulation 4195: submitting
    5s simulation 4195: running (slurm 4137519)
   31s simulation 4195: completed (slurm 4137519)
{ "simulation_id": 4195, "status": "completed", ..., "files": ["out/results_2026-10-07#08-24-19.pber"] }

Or in steps:

$ compose-api run experiment.omex --simulator viva-pde-particle     # prints simulation_database_id
$ compose-api status 4195                                            # "submitting" until the SLURM job exists
$ compose-api wait 4195
$ compose-api results 4195 --extract out/

Once signed in (compose-api auth login), every command sends the profile's session; without one, commands call the API anonymously, as it allows. Neither ever starts a sign-in on its own:

compose-api simulations list                               # with the stored session, or anonymously
compose-api --ephemeral-auth run experiment.omex           # sign in for this one command; keep nothing
  • Simulation ids. A simulation id is what run prints (simulation_database_id), and what status, wait, results, events, trace and datasets list --sim take. To find one later:

console $ compose-api simulations list # newest first, with status and SLURM job $ compose-api simulations list --status running --since 6h $ compose-api simulations list --simulator viva-pde-particle --limit 20 $ compose-api simulations list --label source:biomodels --tag repressilator $ compose-api simulations show 4334 # plus how many events and datasets it recorded

Runs carry labels, written by the service (source, environment, solver, model, ...), and tags and a description given at submission: compose-api run x.omex --tag demo --tag repressilator --description "...". --label key:value and --tag filter the list; each is repeatable, and all must match. - --simulator names a prebuilt simulator image the service is configured with. Without it, the service builds one from the document's dependencies, and build-status <simulator_database_id> follows that build. - status takes several ids and asks for them in one call. - curated copasi and curated tellurium run an SBML model with those simulators. - simulators list, processes list and steps list show what is registered. - openapi --diff reports whether this client and the live service disagree on the API.

docs.title: JSON output
docs.text: Every command takes --json, which prints JSON instead of a table. It's the same as --output json before the command name, and it overrides that option. The auth commands accept --json without listing it in their help: -o json is the spelling documented for them. JSON is also the default whenever output isn't a terminal, so compose-api simulations list | jq needs neither.

docs.title: What a run did: events and traces
docs.text:
Every run records events: the service's own (dispatch.submitted, then slurm.<state> on each change), the job script's (job.start, and job.end with the exit code, inside a job span), and, if the simulator is built on process-bigraph 1.8.5 or later, the engine's (run.start, run.end, process.exception, its spans).

$ compose-api events 4195                  # everything recorded so far
$ compose-api events 4195 --follow         # and new ones as they arrive, until the job has finished
$ compose-api events 4195 --level error    # only what went wrong
$ compose-api trace 4195                   # the spans as a tree, each with its own events
$ compose-api trace 4195 --chrome t.json   # a file for ui.perfetto.dev

With --output json, events prints JSON lines, one event per line. The service reads a run's events while it runs and for a few minutes after it ends, so a --follow may print a last few events after the job is done.

docs.title: What a run produced: datasets
docs.text:
Each file a run leaves in its output/ directory, and its results.zip, is a dataset. The job script records each with its size and sha256 when the run ends. A simulator can announce its own files with an artifact.written event, adding a kind, a name and attributes.

$ compose-api datasets list --sim 4195            # one run's files
$ compose-api datasets list --kind results         # every results file you can read
$ compose-api datasets show <id>
$ compose-api datasets get <id> -O out/            # just that file, not the whole archive

A run's SLURM log is a dataset too (job.out, kind log): compose-api datasets list --sim 4195 --kind log, then datasets get on its id. A dataset is readable by whoever can read its simulation.

docs.title: Output and exit status
docs.text:
Results go to stdout; progress, prompts and human error lines go to stderr. With --json, an error is also printed to stdout as {"error": {"category": ..., "message": ..., "exit_code": ...}}.

Exit Category Meaning 0 Success; with --wait, the job completed 1 not_found, invalid_request, server_error, api_error, job_failed, uncertain, internal The API answered unsuccessfully (404, 400/422, 500, other), the job ended other than completed, a submission outcome was ambiguous, or the CLI hit an internal bug 2 usage A malformed command line, a removed option (--token), or a file argument that cannot be used 3 authentication No session, an expired one that cannot be renewed, a refused or cancelled sign-in, or credentials the API rejected 4 forbidden The API refused the request for this account (403) 5 network, rate_limited, uncertain Auth0 or the API could not be reached, timed out, is unavailable (502/503/504), or is rate limiting (429) 6 configuration, storage, protocol, interaction A profile, credential-store, protocol or local-browser problem 7 wait_timeout --wait-timeout passed before the job finished 130 Cancelled (Ctrl-C)

So compose-api run x.omex --wait && next-step runs next-step only if the simulation completed.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
The command line is a thin layer over compose_api_client.ext, which applications can use directly:

from compose_api_client.ext import ComposeSession

with ComposeSession() as s:  # https://compose.cam.uchc.edu
    sim, state, files = s.run_and_wait("experiment.omex", simulator="viva-pde-particle", dest="out/", extract=True)

AsyncComposeSession has the same methods as coroutines, and AsyncComposeSession.in_process(app) runs against a FastAPI app in a test with no network.

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text:
Drive compose-api: submit simulations, wait for them, fetch results, inspect the catalogue.

Usage:

$ compose-api [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

Options:

  • --url TEXT: Service base URL. [env var: COMPOSE_API_URL]
  • --profile TEXT: Profile to use (default: production). [env var: COMPOSE_API_CLI_PROFILE]
  • --timeout FLOAT: HTTP timeout, seconds (downloads use the full value; other requests cap at 60 s). [env var: COMPOSE_API_TIMEOUT; default: 300.0]
  • -o, --output [auto|table|json]: auto: table on a terminal, else json. [env var: COMPOSE_API_OUTPUT; default: auto]
  • -v, --verbose: Log HTTP requests; tracebacks on errors.
  • -q, --quiet: No progress lines.
  • --ephemeral-auth: Sign in for this command only, keeping credentials in memory (for hosts without a credential store).
  • --method [auto|browser|url|device]: How --ephemeral-auth signs in: auto (device over SSH, else browser), browser, url or device. [default: auto]
  • --version: Print this program's version and exit.
  • --install-completion: Install completion for the current shell.
  • --show-completion: Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

Commands:

  • health: Is the service up, and which version.
  • version: The service's version.
  • catalog: The catalog: every registry entry with its...
  • solvers: The solvers SED-ML runs can use: each...
  • run: Submit a simulation.
  • status: Job state of one simulation, or of several...
  • wait: Wait until each simulation finishes; exit...
  • results: Fetch a finished simulation's results...

Options:

  • --simulator TEXT: A prebuilt simulator image by name (the older form of --environment).
  • --environment TEXT: The environment to run in (environments list); omitted: inferred from the document's classes.
  • --interval FLOAT: Simulation interval passed to the runner. [default: 1.0]
  • --batch / --no-batch: Submit as a batch job (smaller partition, 1 CPU). [default: no-batch]
  • -t, --tag TEXT: A tag to find the run by later (repeatable).
  • --description TEXT: What the run is for.
  • --environment-version INTEGER RANGE: The version of the environment to run in (registry_env@3 is 3); omitted: its default. [x>=1]

  • -d, --download PATH: With --wait: save the results archive into this directory.
  • --extract / --no-extract: With --download: unpack the archive instead of saving the zip. [default: no-extract]
  • --poll FLOAT: Seconds between status checks. [default: 5.0]

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: A proof-of-concept browser UI for this API lives in webapp/. It is a static single-page app built with Nuxt 4, Nuxt UI 4 and Tailwind v4, the same stack as the BioSimulations platform frontend (biosimulations/platform, frontend/), whose shell, theme and page patterns it adapts. The API serves it at /ui on the same host, and / redirects there.

docs.title: What it covers
docs.text:
Page API operations /ui/ dashboard: counts by status, recent runs list-simulations, /version /ui/simulations: paged and filterable by status, simulator, date, labels (key:value) and tags; label and tag chips filter the list; where each run ran ("Ran in"), and the runs of one environment, version or simulator (linked from their pages); download results.zip list-simulations, get-simulation-results-file /ui/simulations/new: upload a .pbg, .omex or .sbml, or a curated COPASI/Tellurium time course from SBML. Registry rejections are listed address by address run-simulation, run-copasi, run-tellurium /ui/simulations/{id}: where it ran (its environment version, or its simulator for a run from before versions), status (polled until terminal), SLURM and container-build details, live event log, span tree and Chrome trace (for Perfetto), datasets with inline previews (images, CSV/TSV plotted with Plotly, JSON, text) get-simulation, get-simulation-status, get-simulator-build-status, get-simulation-events, get-simulation-trace, get-simulation-trace-chrome, list-datasets, get-dataset-content, get-simulation-results-file /ui/datasets: every run's files list-datasets, get-dataset-content /ui/datasets/{id}: one dataset full width in its viewers (a results bundle file by file) get-dataset, get-dataset-content, get-dataset-file /ui/composites/new: write a composite in .pblang, checked as you type, and run it (below) list-environments, get-environment-manifest, run-simulation /ui/sedml: a SED-ML archive (upload, BioModels, biosimulations.org) previewed and run on several solvers (plan-sedml.md) preview-sedml, run-sedml, search-biomodels, get-biomodel-omex, run-biomodel, search-biosimulations-projects, get-biosimulations-omex, run-biosimulations-project, list-solvers /ui/comparisons, /ui/comparisons/{id}: a task's runs, scores per report and data set, overlays of data sets and SED-ML plots list-comparisons, get-comparison, get-comparison-series, list-datasets, get-dataset-content /ui/suites, /ui/suites/{name}: regression and reproducibility suites, their runs (each with the environment versions it ran in), agreement, references and drift from the baseline per model; "Run the suite" (signed in) picks a version of each environment its solvers use and confirms first; with suites:curate, mark, edit and clear each solver's known problems, each confirmed (plan-known-problems) list-suites, list-suite-runs, get-suite-run, run-suite, list-solvers, list-environment-versions, list-suite-problems, mark-suite-problem, edit-suite-problem, clear-suite-problem /ui/environments: where composites run, and the simulators runs used before environments had versions; /ui/environments/{name}: its image, versions (each linked to its runs), registry entries, and every class it provides with its config and ports (#Name opens on one); administration, below list-environments, get-environment-manifest, list-environment-versions, list-simulators /ui/environments/{name}/versions/{n}: one version: its installed packages and a diff against another version, its lock and the pixi/uv files that recreate it, its entries with their compliance cases, its classes, and its runs get-environment-version, export-environment-version, get-environment-version-compliance /ui/simulators/{id}: one simulator (a container definition, identified by its hash): its definition, the versions it is, and its runs. A simulator from before versions belongs to no environment, and this page is the only place it is described get-simulator /ui/catalog: every registry entry with its curation level, pin and evidence, and the environments that run its classes (plan-sedml.md, "Concepts") list-registry-entries

Viewers are registered per dataset type (webapp/app/viewers/registry.ts, plan). Each one declares which datasets it fits (by kind, media type and attributes) and is an async component, so a viewer and its libraries download only when first opened. /ui/datasets/<id> opens a dataset full width; the table's preview shows the same viewers. Built in: composite (below), image, table (plotted when numeric), text, a Plotly figure (application/vnd.plotly.v1+json, SED-ML plots), and for results bundles (*.fenics) a statistics view and a 3D view (vtk.js) read chunk by chunk with zarrita from /datasets/{id}/files/. The 3D view draws the bundle's web extension (a precomputed surface per domain, viva-pde-particle docs/web-bundle.md) coloured by one variable, fetches one row per frame, shows particles, and follows a running simulation.

The submitted composite (the input dataset: a .pbg document, or an OMEX archive holding one or more, found as the service finds them at submission: .pbg and .json members, nested .omex archives at most three deep; with several, a picker chooses one) opens in the composite viewer (webapp/app/viewers/CompositeViewer.vue): the document is decompiled in the browser into .pblang text by process-bigraph-lang (the npm package of its dsl/), checked, and shown read-only in Monaco with the checker's findings as markers and as a list. The Document tab shows the process-bigraph JSON that was submitted and run, re-indented only (every token as submitted: 100.0 stays a float), with a download; the Graph tab draws the wiring (viewers/composite/layout.ts, stores left, processes and steps right, a link per wired port, nested composites below). The checker resolves addresses against interface manifests: one per environment documents run in, generated in CI inside each image and served by the API at GET /registry/environments and GET /registry/environments/{name}/manifest (same origin; in development, from whatever NUXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE points at). The viewer uses the manifest of the environment the run used (a prebuilt run is matched by its image's repository, whatever its digest). Hovering a class's name in the text, or its address in the document, shows the class's interface from that manifest (viewers/composite/interfaces.ts), linked to its environment's page; the "checked against" badge links there too.

Writing a composite (/ui/composites/new, or "Edit a copy" from the viewer) opens .pblang text in an editable Monaco with process-bigraph-lang's language server running in a web worker (viewers/composite/languageClient.ts): findings appear as you type, hover shows a process's interface, and completion offers processes, ports, config keys and stores, all from the manifest of the environment picked above the editor. Run compiles the text in the browser (addresses in the local:module.Class form the service accepts; sidecar files compiled back in) and submits the document as a .pbg to /simulation/run in that environment.

get-simulations-status-batch is not used: it is a GET with a JSON body, which browsers cannot send. The list page re-fetches while any row is still running.

docs.title: How it is built and served
docs.text:
• npm run generate writes static files to webapp/.output/public. The image builds them in a Node stage of Dockerfile-api and copies them in.
  • compose_api/api/webapp.py mounts that directory at /ui when it exists (settings.webapp_dist_dir). A path without a file suffix gets the app shell (200.html), so deep links work. Without a build, the API runs as before.
  • The API calls are typed from the committed OpenAPI spec. npm run types (also run by make clients) regenerates webapp/app/api/schema.d.ts with openapi-typescript, and the calls go through openapi-fetch. CI fails if that file is stale. Never hand-edit it.
  • There is no ingress change: the existing / → api:8000 rule already covers /ui.

docs.title: Sign-in
docs.text:
The API accepts anonymous calls (Authentication), so the UI works without signing in. The UI offers an Auth0 login (@auth0/auth0-vue, after the platform frontend's plugin) only when the API publishes all three of these at GET /webapp/config:

Setting Meaning AUTH0_DOMAIN the tenant, shared with token verification AUTH0_AUDIENCE the API identifier the UI requests a token for AUTH0_SPA_CLIENT_ID an Auth0 Single Page Application whose allowed callback, logout and web origins include https://compose.cam.uchc.edu/ui/ (and http://localhost:4200/ui/ for development), and which may request that audience

Rules for the token:

  • Only API requests carry it: a request gets the token only when its destination is the API's own origin and path (app/utils/apiAuth.ts, after the platform's isPlatformApiRequest), never another host or a lookalike.
  • When the API rejects it (401), the UI drops it, carries on anonymously, and shows a banner. It does not retry.
  • When the session can no longer be renewed (the refresh token expired or was revoked), the UI signs the person out locally and says so, with a button to sign in again.
  • Downloads by a signed-in user are fetched with the token, because a plain link cannot carry the header.
  • After sign-in the UI asks GET /auth/me who the caller is, once. A token the API rejects shows up at once, and the account menu lists the roles the API sees.
  • "Create account" opens Auth0's sign-up page. Signing in returns to the page the person started from.
  • The account menu shows what the API says the caller may do (capabilities from GET /auth/me); with environments:admin it links "You can administer environments".

The token is kept in the browser's local storage, with rotating refresh tokens, as the platform frontend does (decision D1 in plan-webapp-login). Because script injection could read it, every /ui response carries these security headers:

  • A Content-Security-Policy that allows scripts only from this origin, plus the hashes of the build's inline scripts, which the API computes from the files it serves. Connections are allowed only to this origin and the Auth0 tenant. The page cannot be framed. Production enforces it (WEBAPP_CSP_ENFORCE=true); without that setting it only reports. Browsers post violations to POST /webapp/csp-report, which the API logs as CSP violation report.
  • X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy: no-referrer.

A token changes nothing a caller can read, because every simulation is public. It changes what a caller may do only through the capabilities below.

The SPA applications are created by auth0-pulumi (UCHHPC/auth0-pulumi#5): p7uif3ex4LijqPwSOJsPBnhCdClnxSMM for production, whose callbacks also include the dev server's, and fEbf0F5Orb6FD4TySB8yWSZTj5hhBNJV for the local cluster. Their ids are set in kustomize/config/compose-api-rke/api.env and kustomize/overlays/compose-api-local/auth0.env.

docs.title: Administration
docs.text:
Environment versions are administered on the environment's own page (plan-webapp-admin, A2), not in a separate area. The controls appear only when GET /auth/me lists environments:admin, which a caller has when they hold the deployment's ENVIRONMENT_ADMIN_ROLE (production: the tenant's admin role). The UI only displays the capability: the API checks every request again and answers 403 to anyone else, so a hidden button is never the protection.

Action Offered for What it does New version a composed environment (registry_env, a mash-up) resolves its registry entries as of a date (today: now) and locks them, then builds the image and runs its compliance cases; an identical lock gives the existing version Register an image a prebuilt environment registers an image by digest (repository@sha256:…; tags are refused), pulls it and reads it back Make default a ready version that is not the default runs that name no version run in it; recorded runs and suite runs, which name their versions, do not change Retire a ready or failed version that is not the default it refuses new runs; recorded runs keep it, and its images are kept Re-read contents a ready version, or any prebuilt image runs its image again, in the background, to record what it installed and the classes it provides; a build does this by itself, so it is for a prebuilt image or a record that is missing or wrong. Runs and the default are unaffected

Every action is confirmed in a dialog that names the environment, the version and the effect (A3). Making a version the default shows its packages against the current default's (?against=), since a new version changes nothing until it is the default. After a new version is made, the page follows it every five seconds until it is ready or failed, and shows why it failed. Custom library lists are not offered: that path is retired (composition D8.5).

The same actions are compose-api environments create|default|retire|inspect on the command line.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
nvm use                   # Node 24: webapp/.nvmrc, linked from the repo root's .nvmrc (CI reads the same file)
make webapp-install       # npm ci
make run                  # the API on :8000
make webapp-dev           # the UI on http://localhost:4200/ui/, calling the API on :8000
COMPOSE_API_URL=https://compose.cam.uchc.edu make webapp-dev   # against production instead (CORS allows :4200)
make webapp-check         # lint, typecheck, API types current
make webapp-build         # static build; `make run` then serves it at http://localhost:8000/ui/

To sign in from the dev server against make run, set AUTH0_AUDIENCE and AUTH0_SPA_CLIENT_ID in .dev_env as .dev_env_TEMPLATE describes: the production SPA is the only one whose callbacks include http://localhost:4200/ui/.

npm audit reports advisories in build-time tooling (the Nitro dev server and its dependencies). None of it ships: the image serves only the generated static files.

docs.title: Toward one frontend with the platform
docs.text:
The platform frontend is server-rendered and deployed on GKE (biosim.biosimulations.org). This UI is static and served by the API on the on-premise RKE2 cluster (compose.cam.uchc.edu). Because they share a stack, components move between the two without rewriting. There are two ways to reconcile them:

  1. The platform frontend gains a compose backend. These pages become a section of the platform app with a configurable base URL for this API, and /ui here is retired. This needs CORS for the platform origin and the same Auth0 audience setup.
  2. Nuxt layers. These pages ship as a Nuxt layer that both apps extend: the platform app on GKE, and a thin shell here for the on-premise deployment.
